tip: 생각보다 (saenggak-boda) is literally 'than thought' – a ready-made 'than I expected'. Korean compares straight against the noun for your expectation, no verb needed.
Preferences reuse the comparison particle: 여름보다 겨울을 좋아해요 (yeoreum-boda gyeoureul joahaeyo) = like winter more than summer. No separate word for 'more' needed here – 보다 (boda) carries it.
덜 (deol) is the mirror of 더 (deo): 덜 추워요 (deol chuwoyo) = less cold. English rebuilds the sentence with 'not as cold as'; Korean just swaps in 덜.
덜 (deol) = less, dropped right before the adjective: 덜 짜요 (deol jjayo) = less salty. Korean has no '-er' endings – degree words like 덜 and 더 (deo = more) sit before the plain adjective.
-어 주세요 = do it for me: 말해 주세요 (malhae juseyo) = please say it.
제일 (jeil) in front of an adjective makes it 'the most': 제일 맛있어요 (jeil masisseoyo) = the tastiest. Nothing about the adjective changes – the little word does all the work.
-에서 marks the group you are picking the best from: 우리 팀에서 (uri tim-eseo) = on our team.
중에서 (jung-eseo) narrows a 'the most' claim to a group: 가족 중에서 (gajok jung-eseo) = among the family. Without it, 제일 커요 (jeil keoyo) is just 'tallest', with no group named.
가장 (gajang) and 제일 (jeil) both mean 'most', but 가장 leans slightly formal and written – 가장 좋아요 (gajang joayo) sounds a touch more composed than 제일 좋아요 (jeil joayo).
제일 (jeil) and 가장 (gajang) both mean 'most' – 제일 is the everyday spoken choice: 제일 바빠요 (jeil bappayo) = is the busiest.
Popularity is something you have in Korean: 인기가 많아요 (ingi-ga manayo) is literally 'popularity is much'. Friends work the same way – 친구가 많아요 (chingu-ga manayo).
월급날 (wolgeumnal) hides a sound shift: the ㅂ (b) of 월급 (wolgeup) turns into ㅁ (m) before the ㄴ (n) of 날 (nal). Korean smooths consonant clashes like this constantly.
처럼 (cheoreom) means 'like' and glues straight onto the noun: 가수처럼 (gasu-cheoreom) = like a singer. No separate 'as' or 'like' floating in the sentence – the particle carries it.
처럼 (cheoreom) means 'like' but glues onto the end of its noun: 천사처럼 자요 (cheonsa-cheoreom jayo) = sleeps like an angel. English puts 'like' before the noun – Korean tacks it on after.
Materials just take the 'it is' ending -이에요 (-ieyo): 플라스틱이에요 (peullaseutigieyo) = it's plastic.
주말마다 (jumal-mada) = every weekend – 마다 (mada) already carries the 'each and every', so the noun stays singular: no 'weekends' needed.
마음이 바다처럼 넓어요 (maeum-i bada-cheoreom neolbeoyo) – a generous heart is 'wide' in Korean, not big. Wide as the sea is the stock image for a forgiving nature.
Describe people with body word + adjective: 머리가 길어요 (meori-ga gireoyo) = has long hair.
손이 커요 (son-i keoyo), literally 'has big hands' = cooks and serves generously.
Respect extends to a person's traits: 부드러우세요 (budeureouseyo) takes the polite -(으)세요 (-(eu)seyo) because the voice belongs to the 팀장님 (timjangnim). Even their qualities get honored.
-고 (-go) links sentences: 크고 (keugo) = is tall and…
English loans usually turn into verbs with 하다 (hada): 체크인하고 싶어요 (chekeuinhago sipeoyo) is literally 'want to do check-in'. The same trick gives 쇼핑하다 (syopinghada) = to shop.
(으)로 marks the means: 이름으로 (ireum-euro) = under the name.
Nights and days count with Sino numbers: 2박 3일 (i-bak sam-il) = 2 nights, 3 days.
부탁해요 (butakhaeyo) literally asks a favor: 'I entrust this to you'. It turns a bare noun like 방 (bang), room, into a full polite request – no command verb needed.
조식 (josik) is the formal word for breakfast – the one you meet at check-in and on hotel signs. In everyday talk, breakfast is just 아침 (achim), 'morning'.
Clock hours use native numbers: 열한 시 (yeolhan si) = eleven o'clock.
펜션 (pensyeon) is a false friend – in Korea it's a rental holiday guesthouse, a family-trip staple, not a retirement pension. Unlike a hotel room, it usually comes with a kitchen.
보이다 (boida) = be visible: 바다가 보여요 (bada-ga boyeoyo) = the sea is in view.
중이에요 (jung-ieyo) after a noun = in the middle of it: 준비 중이에요 (junbi jung-ieyo) = being prepared.
